mn86:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn86:2.1: 2. Now on that occasion there was a bandit in the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala called Aṅgulimāla, or ‘Finger-garland’ who was murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings.
mn86:2.2: Villages, towns and districts were being laid waste by him.
mn86:2.3: He was constantly murdering people, and he wore their fingers (aṅguli) as a garland (māla).
mn86:3.1: Then, when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Sāvatthi for alms.
mn86:3.2: When he had wandered for alms in Sāvatthi and had returned from his alms-round after his meal, he set his resting place in order, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he set out by the road to where Aṅgulimāla was.
mn86:3.3: Cowherds, shepherds and ploughmen passing by saw him taking the road to where Aṅgulimāla was.
mn86:3.4: When they saw him, they said:
mn86:3.6: On that road is the bandit Aṅgulimāla who is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings.
mn86:3.7: Villages and towns and districts are being laid waste by him.
mn86:3.8: He is constantly murdering people, and he wears their fingers as a garland.
mn86:3.9: Men have come along this road in groups of ten, twenty, thirty and even forty from time to time,
mn86:3.10: but still they have fallen into Aṅgulimāla’s hands.’
mn86:3.11: When this was said the Blessed One went on in silence.
mn86:3.13: A third time the cowherds, shepherds and ploughmen passing by said:
mn86:3.14: ‘Do not take that road, monk. On that road is the bandit Aṅgulimāla who is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings. Villages and towns and districts are being laid waste by him.
mn86:3.15: He is constantly murdering people, and he wears their fingers as a garland.
mn86:3.16: Men have come along this road in groups of ten, twenty, thirty and even forty from time to time,
mn86:3.17: but still they have fallen into Aṅgulimāla’s hands.’
mn86:4.1: Still the Blessed One went on in silence.
mn86:4.2: The bandit Aṅgulimāla saw the Blessed One coming in the distance.
mn86:4.5: Men have come along this road in groups of ten, twenty, thirty and even forty, from time to time
mn86:4.6: but still they have fallen into my hands.
mn86:4.7: And now this monk comes alone and unaccompanied. One would fancy he had been fated to come.
mn86:4.8: Why should I not take this monk’s life ?”
mn86:5.1: Angulimāla took up his sword and shield and buckled on his bow and quiver, and he followed behind the Blessed One.
mn86:5.2: Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernormal success that the bandit Angulimāla, going as fast as he could, was unable to catch up with the Blessed One, who was walking at his normal pace.
mn86:5.5: Formerly I caught up with even a galloping elephant and seized it; I caught up with even a galloping horse and seized it; I caught up with even a galloping chariot and seized it; I caught up with even a galloping deer and seized it;
mn86:5.6: but yet, though I am going as fast as I can, I am unable to catch up with this monk who is walking at his normal pace!’
mn86:5.9: ‘I have stopped, Angulimāla. Do you stop, too.’
mn86:5.11: ‘These monks, sons of Sakyans, speak truth, assert truth:
mn86:5.12: but though this monk is walking yet he says
mn86:5.13: “I have stopped. Angulimāla. Do you stop too.”
mn86:6.1: Then he addressed the Blessed One in stanzas thus:
mn86:6.2: ‘While you are walking, monk, you tell me you have stopped;
mn86:6.3: But now, when I have stopped, you say I have not stopped.
mn86:6.4: I ask you now, O monk, what is the meaning of it;
mn86:6.5: How is it you have stopped and I have not ?’
mn86:6.7: Forswearing violence to every living being;
mn86:6.8: But you have no restraint towards things that breathe:
mn86:6.9: So that is why I have stopped and you have not.’
mn86:6.10: ‘Oh, at long last a sage revered by me,
mn86:6.11: This monk, has now appeared in the great forest:
mn86:6.12: Indeed I will for long renounce all evil,
mn86:6.13: Hearing your stanza showing the Dhamma.’

mn86:6.17: And then and there asked for the Going-forth.
mn86:6.18: The Enlightened One, the Sage of Great Compassion,

mn86:7.1: Then the Blessed One set out to wander by stages back to Sāvatthi with Aṅgulimāla as his attendant monk,
mn86:7.2: and eventually he arrived at Sāvatthi.
mn86:7.3: Then the Blessed One stayed in Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anathapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn86:8.1: Now on that occasion great crowds of people were gathering at the gates of King Pasenadi’s inner palace, very clamorous and noisy, (crying:)
mn86:8.2: ‘Sire, there is a bandit called Aṅgulimāla in your realm; he is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings!
mn86:8.3: Villages, towns and districts are being laid waste by him!
mn86:8.4: He is constantly murdering people, and he wears their fingers as a garland!
mn86:8.5: The king must put him down!’
mn86:9.1: Then in broad day King Pasenadi of Kosala drove out with (a bodyguard of) five hundred horse,
mn86:9.3: He went as far as the road was passable for carriages, and then he dismounted from his carriage and went to the Blessed One on foot. After paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One said to him:
mn86:9.4: ‘What is it, great king? Is Seniya Bimbisāra king of Magadha attacking you, or the Licchavis of Vesāli, or other hostile kings?’
mn86:10.1: ‘Venerable sir, Seniya Bimbisāra king of Magadha is not attacking me, nor are the Licchavis of Vesāli, nor are other hostile kings.
mn86:10.2: But there is a bandit in my realm called Aṅgulimāla, who is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings.
mn86:10.3: Villages, town and districts are being laid waste by him.
mn86:10.4: He is constantly murdering people, and he wears their fingers as a garland.
mn86:10.5: I shall never be able to put him down, venerable sir.’
mn86:11.1: ‘Great king, if you saw that Aṅgulimāla had shaved off his hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and that he was abstaining from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, and from false speech, and, eating in (only) one half of the day, he was living the life divine in virtue and good Dhamma, (if you saw him thus,) how would you treat him?’
mn86:11.2: ‘Venerable sir, we should pay homage, or we should rise up for him, or we should invite him to be seated, or we should invite him to accept robes, alms-food, resting-place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick, or we should arrange for his guarding in accordance with the Dhamma, and his defence and protection.
mn86:11.3: But, venerable sir, he is an evil-doer, one of evil qualities; how could he have such virtue and restraint?’
mn86:12.1: Now on that occasion the venerable Angulimāla was sitting not far from the Blessed One,
mn86:12.2: who extended his right arm, saying to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
mn86:12.4: Then King Pasenadi was alarmed and fearful, and his hair stood on end.
mn86:12.5: Knowing this, the Blessed One told him:
mn86:12.6: ‘Do not be afraid, great king, do not be afraid. There is nothing for you to fear.’
mn86:12.7: Then the king’s alarm and fear and horror was allayed.
mn86:12.8: He went over to the venerable Angulimāla and said:
mn86:12.9: ‘Venerable sir, Angulimāla was a noble lord, was he not?’
mn86:12.11: ‘Venerable sir, of what family was the noble lord’s father? Of what family was his mother?’
mn86:12.12: ‘My father was a Gagga, great king; my mother was a Mantāni.’
mn86:12.13: ‘Let the noble lord Gagga Mantāniputta rest content.
mn86:12.14: I shall take care of robes, alms-food, resting-place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick, for the noble lord Gagga Mantāniputta.’
mn86:13.1: Now on that occasion the venerable Angulimāla was a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater and a refuse-rag wearer restricting himself to three robes.
mn86:13.3: ‘Enough, great king, my triple robe is complete.’
mn86:13.4: King Pasenadi then returned to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said:
mn86:13.5: ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous
mn86:13.6: how the Blessed One subdues the unsubdued, quiets the unquieted, brings about extinguishment in the unextinguished.
mn86:13.7: One whom we, venerable sir, could not subdue with punishments and weapons the Blessed One has subdued without punishment or weapon.
mn86:13.8: And now, venerable sir, we depart;
mn86:13.9: we are busy and have much to do.’
mn86:13.10: ‘It is time now, great king, to do as you think fit.’
mn86:13.11: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he departed.
mn86:14.1: Then when it was morning, the venerable Angulimāla dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Sāvatthi for alms.
mn86:14.2: As he was wandering for alms from house to house in Sāvatthi, he saw a certain woman in travail with a deformed child.
mn86:14.6: When he had wandered for alms in Sāvatthi and had returned from his alms-round after the meal, he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said:
mn86:14.7: ‘Venerable sir, when it was morning I dressed and taking bowl and (outer) robe, I went into Sāvatthi for alms.

mn86:14.10: “What defilement beings suffer; indeed what defilement beings suffer!” ‘
mn86:15.1: ‘In that case, Angulimāla, go into Sāvatthi and say to that woman:
mn86:15.2: “Sister, since I was born I have never purposely deprived a living being of life. By that truth may you and the infant have peace.” ‘
mn86:15.3: ‘Venerable sir, should I not be speaking falsehood in full awareness?
mn86:15.4: For many living beings have been purposely deprived of life by me.’
mn86:15.5: ‘Then, Angulimāla, go into Sāvatthi and say to that woman:
mn86:15.6: “Sister, since I was born with the Noble Birth I have never purposely deprived a living being of life. By that truth may you and the infant have peace.”’
mn86:15.7: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ he replied, and went into Sāvatthi and told the woman:
mn86:15.8: ‘Sister, since I was born with the Noble Birth I have never purposely deprived a living being of life. By that truth may you and the infant have peace.’
mn86:15.9: And the woman and the infant had peace.
mn86:16.1: Then dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent and self-controlled, the venerable Angulimāla, by realization himself here and now entered upon and abode in that supreme goal of the life divine for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
mn86:16.2: He knew directly: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived out, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’
mn86:16.3: And the venerable Angulimāla became one of the Arahants.
mn86:17.1: Then when it was morning, the venerable Angulimāla dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Sāvatthi for alms.
mn86:17.2: Now on that occasion a clod thrown by someone fell on the venerable Angulimāla’s body, and a stick thrown by someone fell on his body, and a potsherd thrown by someone fell on his body.
mn86:17.3: Then with blood running from his broken head, with his bowl broken, and with his outer cloak of patches torn, the venerable Angulimāla went to the Blessed One.
mn86:17.4: The Blessed One saw him coming,
